analysis.one_liner: Lets U.S. banks, finance companies, and insurers indefinitely defer U.S. tax on overseas financing profits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 1999, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently extended a tax exemption letting U.S.-owned banks, finance companies, and insurance companies put off paying U.S. tax on profits from their overseas financing operations until the money is brought back to the U.S. parent company. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action, and it expired at the end of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S.-parented banks, finance companies, and insurers with foreign operations, and their shareholders. They would keep foreign financing profits offshore without paying current U.S. tax — an interest-free deferral from the Treasury that would never expire [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, finance firms, and insurers with foreign operations

how_it_helps.text: Makes the subpart F exemption for active financing income permanent, so U.S. financial firms doing banking or financing business abroad can defer U.S. tax on those earnings until the profits are returned to the U.S. parent [S2].

Strikes the expiration provisions from the tax code for both banking/financing income and foreign insurance income, locking in the deferral for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1998, instead of letting the exemption lapse [S3].
Because tax would be owed only when earnings are repatriated, firms that keep profits offshore indefinitely get what is effectively an interest-free loan from the U.S. Treasury [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, who would forgo federal revenue for as long as financial firms keep their foreign financing profits offshore. Deferral means the tax is delayed indefinitely, not eliminated [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: The U.S. Treasury and general taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Permanently forgoes federal revenue: every year financial firms defer U.S. tax on foreign financing profits, the Treasury collects less, a cost spread across everyone else through higher deficits or other taxes [S2].

Carves out special treatment for financial services income only — other U.S. companies' foreign income remains subject to the subpart F anti-deferral rules — tilting the tax code toward the banking and insurance industries [S2][S3].

Deferral rewards keeping profits outside the United States rather than bringing them home and paying tax; the CRS summary notes the tax applies only when earnings are returned to the U.S. parent company [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated: a specific set of large banks, finance companies, and insurers with overseas operations would get a permanent, open-ended tax deferral. The costs are diffuse — lower federal revenue and a tax code that treats financial income more favorably than other business income. Nothing in the bill offers a measurable benefit to ordinary workers or consumers, so as tax policy it is badly targeted; because it died in committee, no one actually bore those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the Congress and expired when the two-year session ended, without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on April 27, 1999, joined as original cosponsors by Senators Baucus, Mack, Bryan, Murkowski, and Breaux — a bipartisan group [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action recorded [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. financial firms gained nothing, since no permanent deferral was enacted; the Treasury avoided the revenue cost the bill would have created, so general taxpayers are better off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and taxpayers; financial firms gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan backing from the start — of the eight cosponsors, five were Democrats and three were Republicans, and the original group included three Democrats alongside Republican sponsor Hatch — and it died from committee inaction rather than a party split vote [S3][S4].

industries.industry: U.S. banks and finance companies with overseas operations
industries.note: The bill would give them a permanent exemption from the subpart F rules, letting them defer U.S. tax on foreign financing profits indefinitely. The industry's gain comes directly out of federal revenue that other taxpayers would otherwise cover.

The bill strikes the expiration of the insurance-income carve-out in section 953, extending the same deferral benefit to U.S. shareholders of foreign insurance operations. Like the banking provision, its cost is spread across all taxpayers.
